title: Judging, Asking, and Building on the Rock
summary: Jesus warns his disciples not to condemn others while ignoring the beam in their own eye, urges them to ask, seek, and knock because their Father gives good things, and sums up the Law and the Prophets in the command to treat others as they would want to be treated. The sermon closes with a series of choices: the narrow gate or the wide, true prophets or false, saying ‘Lord, Lord’ or doing the Father's will, building on rock or on sand. The crowds are astonished, because Jesus teaches with authority, not like their scribes.
story:
This chapter ends the Sermon on the Mount, the first of the five great blocks of teaching in Matthew's Gospel. Chapter 5 set out the character of the people of the kingdom (the Beatitudes) and the greater righteousness Jesus requires, the Law not abolished but fulfilled. Chapter 6 taught that righteousness before the Father in secret, with the Lord's Prayer at its center, and warned against divided loyalty and anxiety. Chapter 7 turns to how disciples treat one another and outsiders (verses 1 to 12), and then presses every listener to decide (verses 13 to 27). No one who has heard the whole sermon can stay neutral: every hearer is walking one of two roads and building one of two houses, and the storm is coming.

The narrator's closing words (verses 28 and 29) are the first use of a formula that ends each of Matthew's five discourses, and they point both backward and forward. Backward, they gather up the reaction to the sermon: astonishment at a teacher who speaks on his own authority. Forward, they open the next section, in which Jesus comes down from the mountain and shows the same authority in deeds, cleansing a leper, healing at a word, calming a storm, and forgiving sins (chapters 8 and 9). Matthew frames the whole block with nearly identical summaries of Jesus teaching, preaching, and healing (4:23 and 9:35), so that chapters 5 to 7 (the Messiah's word) and chapters 8 and 9 (the Messiah's work) are meant to be read together.
historical:
Matthew's Jesus speaks in Galilee in the late 20s or early 30s AD, in the territory of Herod Antipas, but the Gospel was written for a later audience, most likely in the decades after the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in AD 70; many scholars place it in the 80s, and some earlier. That second setting shows through the chapter. The phrase ‘their scribes’ in verse 29 speaks as though from outside the synagogue of Matthew's day, and the warnings about false prophets and about disciples who work miracles in Jesus' name but do not do the Father's will address a church that already had traveling prophets, charismatic gifts, and people who used Jesus' name without obeying him.

The contrast in verse 29 reflects how Jewish teaching worked. A scribe (grammateus) was an expert in the written Law who taught and applied it, and the respected way to teach was to hand on what one had received. The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, opens its tractate of sayings of the fathers with a chain of tradition: Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly (m. Avot 1:1). Later rabbinic literature is built of rulings attributed to earlier named teachers. Jesus quotes no authorities in the sermon. He sets his own ‘I say to you’ beside what was said (5:22, 28, 32, 34, 39, 44) and here ends by making his own words the foundation of a life (verse 24). Hillel, the leading Pharisaic teacher of the generation before Jesus, who died early in the first century AD, stands behind the most famous parallel to verse 12. The Babylonian Talmud tells how a would-be convert asked to be taught the whole Torah while standing on one foot; Shammai drove him away with the builder's measuring rod in his hand, but Hillel told him that what is hateful to you you should not do to your neighbor, that this is the whole Torah, and that the rest is commentary: go and learn it (b. Shabbat 31a). The Talmud is late (sixth century in its present form), but the story was plainly remembered as Hillel's. The book of Tobit, written in the third or second century BC, gives the same negative form in a father's counsel to his son (Tobit 4:15).

False prophets were a real danger in the first century. Josephus, writing in the 90s, describes a man named Theudas who, under the governor Fadus (about AD 44 to 46), persuaded a crowd to follow him to the Jordan, promising that the river would part at his command; Roman cavalry killed many and beheaded him (Antiquities 20.97-98). Under Felix in the 50s an Egyptian prophet led followers to the Mount of Olives, promising that Jerusalem's walls would fall (Antiquities 20.169-172, Jewish War 2.261-263), and during the burning of the temple in AD 70 a false prophet told the people that God commanded them to go up to the temple to receive signs of deliverance, and thousands died there (Jewish War 6.285-286). The Law itself gave tests for prophets: a prophet who leads the people after other gods is false even if his sign comes true (Deuteronomy 13:1-5), and a word that does not come to pass was not spoken by the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:20-22). Early Christians had to apply such tests. The Didache, a church manual usually dated around AD 100 and possibly from the same region as Matthew, gives instructions on traveling apostles and prophets: a prophet who stays more than two days or asks for money is a false prophet, and not everyone who speaks in the Spirit is a prophet, but only one who has the ways of the Lord (Didache 11:3-12). That last rule is close to ‘by their fruit you will recognize them’.
cultural:
The images of this chapter come from the village and the workshop. The speck (karphos) is a chip, a bit of straw or sawdust; the beam (dokos) is the main timber of a roof. The picture is a deliberate comic exaggeration, a man with a rafter sticking out of his eye offering to do delicate work on his brother's. The rabbis knew a similar proverb. The Babylonian Talmud records Rabbi Tarfon wondering whether anyone in his generation could accept rebuke, since if one says ‘remove the splinter from between your eyes’, the other answers ‘remove the beam from between yours’ (b. Arakhin 16b). The principle of measure for measure in verse 2 was also a Jewish commonplace; the Mishnah says that with the measure a person uses, it is measured to him, and illustrates it from Samson and Absalom (m. Sotah 1:7-8).

Verse 6 would have shocked a Jewish ear. What is holy (to hagion) most naturally means sacrificial meat, which the Law reserved for priests and forbade to outsiders (Exodus 29:33-34, Leviticus 22:10-16). Dogs in Jewish towns were half-wild scavengers, not pets, and pigs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:7). Pearls were among the costliest goods in the ancient world, the kind a merchant would sell everything to buy (13:45-46). To toss consecrated meat to street dogs or pearls to pigs would be both waste and sacrilege. In Jewish speech dogs and pigs could be insults for Gentiles, but Matthew's Gospel ends with a mission to all nations (28:19) and has just told disciples not to condemn, so most interpreters read the saying as about hardened contempt for what is holy, not about any ethnic group.

Bread and fish were the staple foods of Galilee around the lake. A round flat loaf and a stone might look alike (the devil's first temptation had asked Jesus to turn stones into bread, 4:3), and an eel-like fish, or the scaleless creatures that Leviticus 11:10-12 forbade, might suggest a snake. A father's duty to feed his son needed no argument. Jesus' phrase ‘you who are evil’ in verse 11 is striking because it is spoken to disciples: even sinful parents do not give their children stones.

The two ways, one leading to life and one to death, was a familiar pattern in Jewish teaching. Moses sets before Israel life and good, death and evil (Deuteronomy 30:15-20); Jeremiah offers the way of life and the way of death (Jeremiah 21:8); Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous with the way of the wicked. The Didache opens with the words that there are two ways, one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between them (Didache 1:1), and the Jewish apocalypse 4 Ezra, written around AD 100, pictures a city on a broad plain full of good things whose only entrance is a path so narrow that it admits only one person at a time, with fire on one side and deep water on the other (4 Ezra 7:6-9). The same book has the angel tell Ezra that many have been created, but few will be saved (4 Ezra 8:3). A city gate (pulē) was a real bottleneck; the wide road to it carried the traffic of the whole region.

The herding life supplied the sheep and the wolf, and the prophets had already called Israel's corrupt leaders wolves (Ezekiel 22:27, Zephaniah 3:3). Thorns and thistles (akanthai and triboloi in the Greek) are the very pair that the Greek Old Testament uses for the ground's curse in Genesis 3:18. The builders of verses 24 to 27 lived in a land where the rains come in winter, sometimes in violent storms, and where dry stream beds (wadis) can fill in minutes with torrents that sweep away anything built on the loose sand and gravel of their floors. Galilean houses were built of basalt field stones; a careful builder dug down to bedrock, as Luke's version says (Luke 6:48). Ezekiel had pictured the false prophets' flimsy wall, whitewashed to look solid, collapsing in flooding rain and hailstones (Ezekiel 13:10-14), and the rabbis told parables much like this one. In a saying attributed to Elisha ben Abuyah, a person with good deeds who has studied much Torah is like a man who builds first with stones and then with bricks, so that floodwaters cannot move the house, while one who studies without deeds builds with bricks first, and a little water topples it (Avot de-Rabbi Natan A 24). The Mishnah compares one whose wisdom exceeds his deeds to a tree with many branches and few roots that the wind uproots (m. Avot 3:17). Jesus' parable belongs to this world of Jewish wisdom, with one difference: the rock is hearing and doing ‘these words of Mine’.
literary:
The chapter is a sequence of short sayings that gathers into a strong conclusion. Verses 1 to 12 finish the body of the sermon. A warning against condemning others (1 to 5) is balanced at once by a call to discernment (6); an encouragement to prayer argues from lesser to greater, from human fathers to the heavenly Father (7 to 11); and the Golden Rule sums up the Law and the Prophets (12). That phrase repeats 5:17, where the body of the sermon began, and so frames everything between (5:17 to 7:12) as Jesus' fulfilling interpretation of the Scriptures. Dale Allison (The Sermon on the Mount, 1999, and in the commentary he wrote with W. D. Davies) has shown how much of the sermon is built in threes: here three imperatives (ask, seek, knock) are matched by three promises, and the ‘therefore’ of verse 12 draws a conclusion from the whole section rather than from the verses just before it.

Verses 13 to 27 form the conclusion, built of contrasting pairs: two gates and two roads (13 and 14), two kinds of trees and fruit (15 to 20), two kinds of disciples who both say ‘Lord, Lord’ (21 to 23), and two builders (24 to 27). The pairs grow more personal as they go, from roads to people, and the last two end at the judgment. The saying ‘by their fruit you will recognize them’ is repeated at the start and end of verses 16 to 20, framing the section, and verse 19 repeats word for word what John the Baptist said in 3:10, so that Jesus and John preach the same warning. The final parable uses exact repetition: the same rain, torrents, and winds strike both houses, so that the only difference is what each builder did with Jesus' words. The sermon's last word is the house's fall (ptōsis), and the collapse is described as great.

The narrator's comment in verse 28, When Jesus had finished saying these things, closes each of Matthew's five discourses (7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1, 26:1). Benjamin W. Bacon (Studies in Matthew, 1930) argued that the five discourses make Matthew a new Pentateuch, a Christian counterpart to the five books of Moses; few now accept the whole theory, but the formula does echo Deuteronomy, where Moses finishes speaking all these words to Israel (Deuteronomy 31:1, 32:45), and Allison (The New Moses, 1993) has traced how Matthew presents Jesus as a prophet like Moses who is also greater than Moses. Much of the chapter has parallels in Luke, but scattered: the judging sayings and the builders in the Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:37-49), the prayer sayings in Luke 11:9-13, and the narrow door and the people turned away in Luke 13:23-27. Matthew has gathered them into one ordered close.

outline.t: Do not judge: the speck and the beam
The narrow gate and the wide
Lord, Lord: doing the Father's will
The crowds astonished at his authority

doctrines.note: The chapter holds two kinds of judgment together. Disciples must not condemn others, because God will measure them by the measure they use (verses 1 and 2), and yet they must discern false prophets by their fruit (15 to 20). Behind both stands the final judgment, ‘that day’ (verse 22), when Jesus himself declares who belongs to him and the storm tests every house (24 to 27).

Ask, seek, and knock are present imperatives, a call to keep praying (verse 7). The ground of confidence is not the persistence of the one who prays but the character of God, argued from lesser to greater: if sinful parents give their children good things, “how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him” (verse 11).

The Golden Rule (verse 12) gives the command to love one's neighbor (Leviticus 19:18) a practical measure: the good one wants for oneself. Jesus calls it the Law and the Prophets, as he will later say that all the Law and the Prophets hang on the two commands to love God and neighbor (22:40).

Calling Jesus Lord, even doing mighty works in his name, is not the same as belonging to him (verses 21 to 23). Faith that is real hears his words and does them (24); the tree is known by its fruit. The chapter does not teach salvation by works, but it refuses a faith that makes no difference to how one lives.

The closing parable is wisdom teaching in the tradition of Proverbs and of Jewish sages who compared study without deeds to a house on a weak foundation. The wise (phronimos) person hears and does; the fool (mōros) hears and does not, and the difference shows only when the storm comes.

words.note: Krinō, to judge. It occurs about 114 times in the New Testament, with a range that BDAG, the standard lexicon, sets out from separating and selecting, through forming an opinion and evaluating, to passing judgment in court and condemning. The same chapter requires discernment about what is holy (verse 6) and about false prophets (15 to 20), and Jesus later tells a brother to confront one who sins against him (18:15), so verse 1 cannot forbid all moral assessment. What it forbids is the verdict of condemnation passed by someone who excuses himself, the sense the word also has in Romans 2:1 and 14:4, and the warning is that God will use the same measure on the judge.

Hupokritēs, hypocrite. The word first meant a stage actor, one who plays a part behind a mask. It occurs eighteen times in the New Testament, fourteen of them in Matthew, where it is Jesus' charge against those who perform righteousness for show (6:2, 6:5, 6:16) and, later, against scribes and Pharisees (23:13-29). In verse 5 the word is turned on disciples: the one who corrects a brother while ignoring his own fault is playing the part of a physician.

Aiteō, to ask or request. It occurs about seventy times in the New Testament, fourteen in Matthew, often of prayer (6:8, 18:19, 21:22) and of a child asking a parent. In verses 7 to 11 it appears five times, beginning with a present imperative (keep asking) and ending with the Father who gives to those who ask. The verb frames the passage: the whole argument turns on what kind of father is being asked.

Stenos, narrow. It occurs only three times in the New Testament: twice here and once in Luke 13:24, the narrow door. In verse 14 it is joined to tethlimmenē, the perfect participle of thlibō, to press or crowd (G2346), the verb behind thlipsis, affliction or tribulation. The road to life is not only narrow but hemmed in, a way of pressure, which fits the persecution the sermon promised (5:10-12). The picture is of a demanding road that must be found and walked, not of a God reluctant to admit people.

Karpos, fruit. It occurs about sixty-six times in the New Testament and nineteen times in Matthew, more than in any other book, and seven times in this chapter. Matthew uses it for the visible outcome of a life: John demands fruit worthy of repentance (3:8), the good soil yields a crop (13:23), and the kingdom will be given to a people producing its fruit (21:43). Here it is the test of prophets and of every disciple, what a life actually produces over time rather than what it claims.

Ginōskō, to know. It is one of the commonest verbs in the New Testament (about 222 times). In verse 23 it carries the Old Testament sense of a relationship God initiates, as in Amos 3:2, where the LORD says Israel alone he has known among the families of the earth, and Jeremiah 1:5. ‘I never knew you’ does not mean Jesus was unaware of these people; it means he never owned them as his. Paul uses the verb the same way when he says it matters more to be known by God than to know (1 Corinthians 8:3, Galatians 4:9).

Anomia, lawlessness. It occurs fifteen times in the New Testament, four in Matthew, and only Matthew among the Gospels uses it. It names not ignorance of the Law but a life that disregards God's will, even behind a religious appearance: the scribes and Pharisees are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness within (23:28), and in the last days lawlessness will increase and love grow cold (24:12). The phrase ‘workers of lawlessness’ echoes Psalm 6:8 (6:9 in the Greek Old Testament), where the psalmist tells evildoers to depart from him.

Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. It occurs about 102 times in the New Testament and ten in Matthew. The crowds notice that Jesus teaches on his own authority rather than by citing earlier teachers (verse 29), and the next two chapters show the same authority over disease (8:9) and over sin (9:6, 9:8). The word returns at the Gospel's climax, when the risen Jesus claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18) and sends his disciples to teach all nations to obey what he commanded.

christ:
The end of the sermon makes the startling scope of Jesus' claim plain. He says that ‘on that day’, the prophets' phrase for the day of the LORD's judgment (Isaiah 2:11, Zechariah 14:4), many will stand before him and appeal to what they did in his name, and he will be the one to declare, “I never knew you; depart from Me, you workers of lawlessness!” In the Old Testament the LORD is the judge of all the earth (Genesis 18:25, Psalm 96:13); here Jesus speaks as that judge, and the standard is whether he knew them. For the first time in the sermon he speaks of ‘My Father’ (verse 21) rather than ‘your Father’, a claim to a unique sonship that the Gospel will unfold (11:27).

He also makes his own words the foundation of life: everyone who hears “these words of Mine” and acts on them builds on the rock. In the Old Testament God himself is Israel's rock (Deuteronomy 32:4, Psalm 18:2, Isaiah 26:4), and Moses called Israel to hear and do the words of the LORD (Deuteronomy 5:1, 30:11-14). Jesus puts his own teaching where Moses put God's. That is why the crowds are astonished: he does not argue from the tradition but speaks as the one to whom the tradition pointed. Later he will say that heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not (24:35).

The rest of the Gospel shows this authority confirmed in his healings and forgiveness (chapters 8 and 9), in his death, and in his resurrection, after which he claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18). He also lived the chapter. He asked the Father and was heard, and in Gethsemane he asked and submitted (26:39). He did not condemn the sinners who came to him, but he did not hide their need of repentance (9:12-13). He did to others, including his enemies, what no one did for him, and he walked the narrow and afflicted road to the cross. The Golden Rule, which no one keeps, is fulfilled by the one who gave his life as a ransom for many (20:28).
interpretation:
The chapter's sayings were among the first words of Jesus the church repeated. The Didache opens with the two ways (1:1), gives the Golden Rule in its negative form, whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to another (1:2), applies ‘do not give what is holy to the dogs’ to keeping the Eucharist for the baptized (9:5), and tests prophets by their conduct (11). The sermon called 2 Clement, from the mid-second century, cites the saying that not everyone who says ‘Lord, Lord’ will be saved, but the one who does righteousness (2 Clement 4:2), and Justin Martyr (First Apology 16, around AD 155) quoted verses 15 to 23 to the emperor as a warning that those who do not live as Christ taught are not truly Christians. Hilary of Poitiers wrote the oldest surviving Latin commentary on Matthew around 350, and John Chrysostom preached ninety homilies on Matthew at Antioch around 390. Augustine's two books On the Lord's Sermon on the Mount (around 393 to 394) gave the sermon the name it still bears; he read verse 6 as a warning against exposing sacred truths to people who will mock them, and he ended his Confessions (13.38) with the words of verse 7, asking, seeking, and knocking at God's door.

The Golden Rule had a long public life. Gratian's Decretum, the foundation of medieval canon law (around 1140), opens by defining natural law as what is contained in the Law and the Gospel, by which each is commanded to do to another what he would have done to himself and forbidden to do what he would not, and scholastic theology treated the rule as the summary of natural law. Immanuel Kant (Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, 1785) objected in a footnote that the negative form cannot serve as a universal moral law, since it contains no duties to oneself, no duty of benevolence, and would let a criminal argue against the judge who sentences him. Albrecht Dihle (Die Goldene Regel, 1962) traced the rule through Greek popular ethics as an ethic of reciprocity, and Jeffrey Wattles (The Golden Rule, 1996) wrote its first full history in English in centuries. Jewish scholars pushed back against Christian claims that the positive form proved Jesus' ethic superior to Judaism's: Kaufmann Kohler's article on the Golden Rule in the Jewish Encyclopedia (1901 to 1906) argued that the principle had been taught authoritatively in Israel before Jesus and that Hillel's other sayings, such as his call to love one's fellow creatures (m. Avot 1:12), show he did not restrict it to Jews.

The opening command has had a stormy history of its own. Leo Tolstoy (What I Believe, 1884) concluded that ‘judge not’ forbids Christians to take part in law courts at all, since human tribunals contradict ‘resist not evil’. Martin Luther, whose sermons on Matthew 5 to 7 were preached from 1530 and published in 1532, answered that the command binds the private person and does not abolish the office of judge, parent, or preacher, who must judge for the sake of others; John Calvin's Harmony of the Gospels (1555) said the same, and warned against the censorious spirit that watches for others' faults. John Wesley devoted the last four of his thirteen discourses on the Sermon on the Mount (Sermons 30 to 33) to this chapter, ending with a searching sermon on verses 21 to 27 about the religion of words and the religion of obedience. Dietrich Bonhoeffer (Discipleship, 1937) read the chapter as the disciple's refusal to stand over others and the call to obey the words, not merely admire them. In the twentieth century John Stott (Christian Counter-Culture, 1978) and Martyn Lloyd-Jones (Studies in the Sermon on the Mount, 1959 to 1960) shaped evangelical preaching on the chapter, and the commentaries of W. D. Davies and Dale Allison (1988), Hans Dieter Betz (The Sermon on the Mount, 1995), and Ulrich Luz (Hermeneia, 2007) set it in its Jewish and Greco-Roman setting and traced its reception.

In worship, the Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 21 to 29 in Year A (Proper 4, or the ninth Sunday after the Epiphany), and the Roman Lectionary reads verses 21 to 27 on the ninth Sunday in Ordinary Time in Year A, paired with Moses' blessing and curse (Deuteronomy 11:18, 26-28, 32). The two builders have become one of the best-known children's teaching stories in the church, and the phrases ‘judge not’, ‘ask, and it shall be given you’ (in the King James wording), ‘a wolf in sheep's clothing’, ‘by their fruits ye shall know them’, and ‘pearls before swine’ passed into ordinary English.
text:
A few differences between English Bibles come from the manuscripts, and one from translation. In verse 2 the Textus Receptus, the Greek text behind the King James Version, reads a compound verb meaning ‘it will be measured back to you’ (the KJV's ‘it shall be measured to you again’), where the earlier manuscripts have the simple verb. In verse 13 the original hand of Codex Sinaiticus and some Old Latin witnesses lack the word ‘gate’ in the second clause, reading ‘wide and broad is the way’; the major editions print it. In verse 14 the manuscripts divide between hoti, ‘because’, which the King James Version follows (‘Because strait is the gate’), and ti, an exclamation, ‘how narrow is the gate’, which the Nestle-Aland text prints; the BSB's ‘But small is the gate’ avoids deciding. The KJV's ‘strait’ is not a misspelling of ‘straight’ but an old English word for narrow.

In verse 24 the later Byzantine manuscripts and the King James Version read ‘I will liken him’, while the earlier manuscripts have ‘he will be like’; the sense is the same. In verse 29 the earliest manuscripts read ‘their scribes’; many later ones read simply ‘the scribes’, as in the King James Version, and some add ‘and the Pharisees’. Verse 12 carries a translation choice rather than a manuscript difference. The Greek says ‘for this is the Law and the Prophets’; the BSB's “the essence of” and the NIV's ‘sums up’ interpret the sense, while the ESV and KJV keep the bare ‘this is’. English versions also differ on the translation of verse 6's final clause: the Greek puts the trampling in the future indicative after mēpote, ‘lest’, which states the likely result, and on who does the tearing, which grammar leaves to the reader (probably the dogs, if the verse is a chiasm).

teach.big: The one who will judge the world tells his disciples not to condemn, to pray with a child's confidence, to treat others as they would want to be treated, and to build their lives on doing his words, because on that day only what is built on him will stand.

outline.t: Refuse the self-righteous verdict: deal with your own beam first, and then you will see clearly enough to help your brother, which remains the goal.
Not condemning is not the same as not discerning: holy things are not to be handed to those who will trample them.
Keep asking, seeking, and knocking, because the one you ask is a Father who gives good things, better than the best human parent.
Let the good you want for yourself be the measure of what you do for others; this is what the Law and the Prophets were aiming at.
The road to life is narrow and pressured and must be found; the crowd is not a safe guide.
Test teachers by the fruit of their lives and teaching over time, not by their clothing, confidence, or gifts.
Religious words and even mighty works cannot substitute for being known by Jesus and doing the Father's will.
The same storms come to everyone; the difference is whether we have built on hearing and doing Jesus' words.
Jesus speaks with an authority of his own, and the right response is not admiration alone but obedience.

teach.pitfalls:
The most common misuse of this chapter is ‘judge not’ used as a shield: a demand that no one name wrong at all, often from the person who has done it. The chapter itself requires discernment about the holy and about false prophets, and Matthew later gives a process for confronting sin in the church (18:15-17). What Jesus forbids is the hypocrite's verdict, not moral clarity. The opposite misuse is just as common: skipping verses 1 to 5 to get to verse 6, and treating people as dogs and pigs whenever they resist. The order of the text matters; beam before speck, and then help, not contempt.

Verses 7 to 11 are often taught as a blank check, as if persistence guaranteed any request. The promise is grounded in the Father's goodness, and a good father sometimes gives what the child did not ask for; Luke's version names the best gift as the Holy Spirit (Luke 11:13). Do not tell people their prayers failed because they asked too little. Verse 12 is sometimes presented as proof that Christianity's ethic is uniquely positive and Judaism's merely negative; that claim overreaches, since Leviticus 19:18 commands love of neighbor and Jewish teachers used both forms, as did early Christians (Didache 1:2). Verses 13 and 14 can be turned into a boast that a small group must be right, or into a numbers game about how many will be saved; Jesus refused that question when it was put to him (Luke 13:23-24) and turned it into a call to enter. Verses 15 to 20 do not license suspicion of every leader or a hunt for heretics by gossip; fruit takes seasons to show, and the tests are Scripture's tests. Finally, verses 21 to 27 are not a call to earn salvation by effort. The sermon opened by blessing the poor in spirit (5:3), and the rock is Jesus' words, which include his call to the weary (11:28-30).
teach.pastoral: Two opposite kinds of people will be in the room. Some have been harmed by others and then told ‘judge not’ when they tried to name it; they need to hear that Jesus does not forbid calling abuse, fraud, or cruelty what it is, and that reporting harm, seeking safety, and protecting others are not the condemnation he forbids. Others are scrupulous, people whose consciences never rest, who will hear verses 21 to 23 and fear that they are among those Jesus never knew. Speak to them plainly: the people turned away in verse 23 are confident, pointing to their achievements, and do not ask whether they are known; a person anxiously asking whether Christ will receive them is not their portrait. Assurance rests on Christ's word and promise (11:28), not on the strength of one's feelings or the completeness of one's obedience, and pastoral care for scrupulosity may include counsel from a trusted pastor or a qualified professional. Verses 7 to 11 will press on those whose prayers for a child, a marriage, or a healing seem unanswered, and on those whose own fathers gave them stones. Let the text's comparison run in the direction it runs: God is better than the best father, not like the worst.

hard.q: Is Jesus' positive Golden Rule really different from, or better than, Hillel's negative form?
hard.a:
The objection has been pressed from several sides. Jewish scholars have long protested Christian claims, common in nineteenth-century preaching, that Jesus' positive rule (do to others) shows an ethic superior to Hillel's negative one (do not do to your neighbor what is hateful to you, b. Shabbat 31a) or to Tobit's (Tobit 4:15). Kaufmann Kohler, in the Jewish Encyclopedia, argued that the principle had already been taught authoritatively in Israel, that Hillel's own call to love all creatures (m. Avot 1:12) shows its breadth, and that Leviticus 19:18 is the source of both forms. Historians note that the negative form appears in Christian texts too (Didache 1:2) and that Gratian's Decretum joins both forms as one natural law. Philosophers have raised a different objection to the rule itself: Kant (1785) argued that it cannot ground morality because it depends on what an individual happens to want, and a critic can ask whether a masochist or a fanatic should do to others what he wants done to himself. Albrecht Dihle (1962) traced the rule to the ethics of reciprocity, give as you expect to get, which Jesus elsewhere criticizes (Luke 6:32-34).

Responses begin by conceding much of this. Christian scholars such as W. D. Davies and Dale Allison and Ulrich Luz grant that the difference between the negative and positive forms has been overstated, that both appear in Jewish and non-Jewish sources, and that Jesus stands within Judaism here, as his own reference to the Law and the Prophets insists. What many still see as distinctive is the rule's setting. In Matthew it follows the command to love enemies and pray for persecutors (5:44), and it is grounded not in reciprocity but in the Father who gives good things to those who ask (verse 11); the ‘therefore’ ties the rule to God's generosity, not to what one expects back. Against Kant's objection, defenders such as Jeffrey Wattles (1996) argue that the rule was never meant to stand alone as a complete theory of ethics but to work within a larger moral and religious framework, here the whole sermon, which supplies what the rule by itself lacks. Hillel's own words, the rest is commentary: go and learn it, point in the same direction. Readers who agree on the substance may still differ on how much weight the positive form carries, and the question is best taught as a place where Jesus and the best of his Jewish contemporaries meet.

hard.q: Does the narrow gate mean few will be saved, and if people who did miracles in Jesus' name are turned away, can anyone be sure?
hard.a:
The objection comes in two forms. The first is moral. Bertrand Russell (Why I Am Not a Christian, 1927) counted Jesus' belief in everlasting punishment and his warnings of weeping and gnashing of teeth a defect in his moral character, and many readers find it hard to believe that a good God would let most of humanity walk the wide road to destruction. Jewish tradition answers the question of numbers differently: the Mishnah says that all Israel has a share in the world to come, with named exceptions (m. Sanhedrin 10:1), though the apocalypse 4 Ezra, near Matthew in date, is as stark as this chapter (4 Ezra 8:3). The second form is pastoral. If people who prophesied, cast out demons, and did many miracles in Jesus' name are told “I never knew you”, then gifts, experiences, and confessions prove nothing, and a sensitive reader may conclude that no one can know where they stand. John Bunyan's account of his years of terror over whether he was saved (Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, 1666) shows how such texts can torment the scrupulous.

On numbers, many interpreters note that Jesus declined to give a count when asked (Luke 13:23-24) and that ‘many’ and ‘few’ here function as prophetic warning against following the crowd rather than as a census of eternity; others, following Augustine and much of the Reformed tradition, take the words as a sober statement that the saved are fewer than the lost. Christians also differ on hell itself, between eternal conscious punishment, conditional immortality, and hopeful universalism, and those positions are discussed in the site's doctrine study of hell and final destinies. On assurance, the traditions answer differently. The Reformed tradition (Westminster Confession, 1646, chapter 18) teaches that true believers may have an infallible assurance grounded in God's promises, the inward evidence of grace, and the witness of the Spirit, and reads verses 21 to 23 as describing people who were never converted, since Jesus says he never knew them, not that he stopped knowing them. The Wesleyan tradition speaks of the witness of the Spirit (Wesley's sermons on that theme) while holding that believers can fall away through persistent sin. The Council of Trent (Session 6, chapters 9 and 12, 1547) rejected a presumptuous certainty of one's own final perseverance apart from special revelation while commending firm hope in God's mercy. Across these views there is agreement on two points the text itself makes. The people in verse 22 rest their case on their own works (‘did we not’), and the chapter's remedy is not introspection but hearing and doing Jesus' words, which begin with the blessing of the poor in spirit and the invitation to ask the Father.

observe: What reason does Jesus give in verse 2 for not judging, and what does he say must happen before a person can help a brother with a speck?
In verses 7 to 11, what three commands and three promises does Jesus give, and what comparison does he use to support them?
List the contrasting pairs in verses 13 to 27. What is the one difference between the two builders?
interpret: How can verse 1 forbid judging while verses 6 and 15 to 20 require discernment? What exactly is Jesus forbidding?
Why do you think Jesus calls the Golden Rule the Law and the Prophets, and how does it relate to loving God and neighbor in 22:37-40?
The people in verses 22 and 23 did real things in Jesus' name. What does ‘I never knew you’ reveal about what they lacked?
apply: Whose faults are you quickest to notice, and what might be the beam in your own eye in that relationship?
Think of one person you find difficult. What would you want from them if your places were reversed, and what would it mean to do that for them this week?
Both houses faced the same storm. What storms have tested what your life is built on, and which of Jesus' words have you heard but not yet acted on?
